source: Smyth and Keane (1994/95) Experiments on adaptation-guided retrieval in case-based design (TCD-CS-94-17)
finding: Ranking cases by similarity does not find the case that is easiest to adapt. Ranking by estimated adaptation cost (AGR) did. Tested in Deja Vu, a software-design CBR system for plant control.
numbers: Expt 1, 45 target problems. Trial 1 (45 cases, one plant model): AGR picked the most adaptable case 100%, standard similarity (SS) 70% (chi2(1)=14.3, p<.0001). Trial 2 (120 cases, 8 plant models): AGR 100%, SS 12% (chi2(1)=65.3).
quote: Standard CBR systems use semantic-similarity to retrieve cases, on the assumption that the most similar case is the best or easiest case to adapt.
limits: One domain (plant-control software design), a symbolic system with hand-built adaptation knowledge. SS failed because exact entity matches pulled in same-model cases that were harder to adapt. Authors concede a better-weighted SS could narrow the gap. No LLM adapter.
agent_relevance: Closes the classic-paper-unread part of gap 3. Warns that the most surface-similar past case may be a worse base to edit than a structurally different one. For an LLM the cost-to-adapt model is missing; it would have to be an LLM judgment or a learned score.

source: Smyth and Keane (1994/95) same report, Expt 2 and 3
finding: AGR keeps retrieval cost from growing with case-base size because only adaptable cases are examined, and it makes total problem solving faster.
numbers: Expt 2: case-base 30 to 120 cases, retrieval time grows but not linearly; flat when number of adaptable cases held at 3. Expt 3: 100 cases, 45 problems; AGR system 120 s total (mean 2.07 s, SD 2.07) vs similarity-then-adapt system 280 s (mean 6.22 s, SD 5.66); t(44)=5.65, p<.0001.
limits: Measures solving time of a symbolic system, not solution quality of an LLM. Gains depend on a usable adaptation-cost model.
agent_relevance: At the token level the analogue is: spend a cheap call to rank k candidate cases by edit effort before one full reuse call. Untested for LLMs.

source: Hatalis et al. (2025) Review of case-based reasoning for LLM agents (arXiv 2504.06943)
finding: Survey of CBR plus LLM agents. It describes hybrid retrieval, adaptation operators and meta-cognitive case selection, and cites reported gains, but reports no experiment of its own. I found no adaptation-cost-ranked retrieval for LLMs in it.
numbers: None of its own. It repeats third-party claims (e.g. DS-Agent 100% development-stage success, 99% one-pass deployment with GPT-4).
limits: Survey with formulas and no new data. Its Wilkerson 2024 mentions are about explanation and trust (nearest neighbour plus stated differences scored highest on trust), not about 20-28% case-choice agreement.
agent_relevance: Confirms gap 3 and gap 8 are still open in the literature the survey covers. Do not cite it for numbers.

source: Yin and Leake (2026) Capturing LLM cases for RAG reuse (ICCBR'26 workshop, PRIM)
finding: The LLM's own past answers plus right/wrong feedback are stored as cases and the single nearest case is put in the next prompt. Gains are small and uneven across 6 models and 3 MMLU subsets. A second round of feedback (store only successes) did not reliably help.
numbers: MMLU history 687, science 750, math 548 questions. Retrieval: bge-small-en-v1.5, L2 in FAISS, k=1 case. Examples (baseline to single feedback): Llama-3.1-8B history 76.9 to 82.1, math 58.0 to 60.9; Llama-70B history 89.1 to 90.5, science 86.5 to 86.5, math 82.3 to 82.5; Qwen2.5-32B math 89.8 to 90.7. 4 trials significant for single vs baseline, 3 for double vs single, 6 trials where double feedback lowered accuracy (not significant). Table text was garbled in extraction so read per-cell values with care.
limits: Multiple-choice knowledge questions, not multi-step reasoning. No random-case control, no variance across seeds, McNemar test only. Strong models gain 0 to 1 point.
agent_relevance: Best k=1 own-experience test found for gap 1, but it has no random-case arm. Gain shrinks as model strength rises: near zero for 70B and 32B models on science and math.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: experience-following (arXiv 2505.16067), Sec 3.3
finding: Agents copy what they retrieve. When the input of a retrieved record is very similar to the current task, the agent's output is very similar to the stored output (experience-following). Measured on 4 agents and with GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 backbones.
numbers: Input similarity = highest cosine of retrieved inputs (text-embedding-3-large); output similarity = code-plagiarism score or embedding similarity. Output similarity rises with input similarity under all add-strategies; with a strict evaluator in RegAgent the paper describes near-perfect correlation (Pearson r near 1). Fixed small memory (100 records) shows lower input and output similarity.
limits: Correlational. Curves reported as cumulative averages in figures; exact r values only stated qualitatively in the text I read. Agents are task-specific (regression, EHR code, driving, IoT).
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 2: near-duplicate retrieved cases do get copied. So the stored solution quality, not just similarity, decides the result.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) same paper, Table 1 and Sec 3.4 error propagation
finding: Storing every run (add-all) makes agents worse than a small fixed memory. A strict (ground-truth) filter makes them better. Errors in stored runs propagate: the same retrieved examples with ground-truth outputs substituted beat the real memory from the first step.
numbers: Table 1, fixed memory vs add-all vs strict: RegAgent SR 67.53 vs 55.48 vs 70.95 (memory 100 vs 4100 vs 2938); EHRAgent ACC 16.75 vs 13.05 vs 38.50; AgentDriver SR 40.11 vs 32.32 vs 51.00; CIC-IoT 71.50 vs 59.90 vs 85.40. Coarse LLM evaluators C1/C2/C3 land between (RegAgent 63.18/65.78/67.35). Error-free replay gap appears immediately and widens for add-all and coarse filters; with strict addition AgentDriver closes the gap and passes it after about 2000 executions.
limits: Strict evaluator = human or exact-match ground truth, not available online. C3 evaluator was fine-tuned on 300 trajectories. No random-case arm.
agent_relevance: Strongest measured evidence for gap 2 and gap 10: add-all lowers success by 8 to 12 points versus no growth; wrong stored solutions are copied. Gate memory writes on verified outcomes.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) same paper, Sec 4 deletion, Table 2
finding: Deleting stored records whose past retrievals led to poor outcomes (history-based deletion, utility threshold, at least n retrievals) is reported to help most with a reliable evaluator. Periodic frequency-based deletion cuts memory about 3x with a small loss.
numbers: RegAgent coarse-C1 add: no deletion 63.18 (3511 records), periodic 60.88 (1012), history 62.10 (3205), combined 59.32 (951). RegAgent strict add: 70.95 (2938), periodic 67.65 (949), history 69.80 (2286), combined 66.58 (890). Settings: at least 5 retrievals, utility threshold 0.5 (0.3 or 0.7 by agent). I read only the RegAgent block of Table 2 in full.
limits: On RegAgent history deletion did not beat no-deletion in the rows I read; the paper reports gains for other agents. Utility is the next-task outcome, noisy with few retrievals.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 and 10: a usable online utility signal exists (average outcome when retrieved), but needs a minimum of about 5 retrievals per case. That is a floor for tiny banks of tens of cases.

source: Mallen et al. (2023) When not to trust language models (ACL 2023, arXiv 2212.10511)
finding: Retrieval helps on rare (long-tail) facts and hurts on popular ones the model already knows. A gate based only on the question (entity popularity vs a threshold) beat always-retrieve and never-retrieve.
numbers: PopQA. Retrieval made the LM wrong on 10% of questions it otherwise got right (recall@1 on those only 0.14 vs 0.42 overall); it rescued 17% of questions (recall@1 0.88). Adaptive retrieval with GPT-3 davinci-003 plus GenRead and Contriever: 46.5% accuracy, 5.3 points above any non-adaptive method. Abstract: up to 10% gain and lower inference cost.
limits: Factoid QA with Wikipedia retrieval and a popularity proxy; GPT-3 era models. Not case reuse for reasoning.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the one measured example of a skip-retrieval rule. Harm region = cases where the model already knows the answer or retrieval quality is low (recall@1 0.14). Analogue for cases: skip when top similarity is low or the task is easy.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Active retrieval augmented generation (FLARE, arXiv 2305.06983), threshold analysis
finding: Trigger retrieval only when the model next sentence has low-confidence tokens. Retrieving at every step is not needed and can hurt.
numbers: Sweep of confidence threshold from 0 to 1: on 2WikiMultihopQA performance plateaus once retrieval fires on more than 60% of sentences; on StrategyQA performance drops when retrieval fires on more than 50% of sentences. Retrieving for 40-80% of sentences was good across tasks.
limits: Token-probability confidence needs logprob access. Tasks are open-domain QA.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a confidence gate has measured support in QA: retrieval at 100% is not best on one of two datasets. Needs logprobs or a verbalised confidence for a frontier API agent.

source: Yoran et al. (2024) Making retrieval-augmented language models robust to irrelevant context (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.01558)
finding: Irrelevant retrieved text is often copied. Even a strong top-1 retriever hurt Llama-2-13B (few-shot) on two of five tasks, and a random passage dropped accuracy sharply on all five.
numbers: 500 dev examples per dataset. StrategyQA and Fermi: top-1 Google retrieval worse than no retrieval. Random passage: average drop of more than 10 points for in-context RALM; an NLI filter removes most of the harm but also the gains; fine-tuning on a mix of relevant and irrelevant contexts (1000 examples enough) restores robustness. Error analysis lists copying irrelevant answers and hallucinated decompositions.
limits: Llama-2-13B, QA with multi-hop decomposition. Exact per-dataset numbers are in figures I did not transcribe.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and 2: supports a relevance gate plus a verification step. Harm from a wrong or random context is large in multi-step tasks, which is the target regime.

finding: A small classifier predicts query complexity and routes among no retrieval, single-step retrieval, and multi-step retrieval. This beat fixed strategies on accuracy per time. A simple retrieve-or-not router was weak on multi-hop sets.
numbers: Labels built automatically from which strategy gets the answer right (cheapest first). Oracle classifier gives best accuracy at far lower time than always multi-step. Paper text states the real classifier leaves a gap to the oracle. GPT-3.5 handles simple queries well without retrieval but benefits on multi-hop queries. Table cells not copied.
limits: Models FLAN-T5 and GPT-3.5, QA datasets. Trained classifier, not a similarity threshold.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a router can be trained from the agent own run log (which strategy worked) without human labels. Binary skip-vs-retrieve is not enough for hard multi-step queries.

source: An et al. (2023) Skill-based few-shot selection, Skill-KNN (EMNLP 2023 Findings, arXiv 2305.14210)
finding: Replacing the raw problem text with an LLM-written description of the skills the problem needs, then embedding that, picks better examples than raw-input embedding. Needs no training.
numbers: Spider (text-chat-davinci-002): Skill-KNN 78.3 execution accuracy vs best raw-input method 74.6 and oracle Target-KNN 78.6. Text-davinci-003 Spider: Random 72.9, KNN-SBERT 73.0, KNN-Ada 72.8, Skill-KNN SBERT 76.8 (78.3 with distinctiveness), Skill-KNN Ada 77.1. COGS: KNN-SBERT 88.3 vs Skill-KNN about 94. On Dr. Spider perturbations, raw SBERT-KNN fell below Random on 2 of 3 perturbation types while Skill-KNN stayed above Random.
limits: Semantic parsing (SQL, COGS), Codex and GPT-3.x models. A math-reasoning side test exists but I did not extract it. Rewriting costs one extra LLM call per case and per query.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: best direct evidence that an LLM-written abstract of problem structure beats raw text as a key. Also shows raw-text similarity can fall below random under perturbation (bears on gap 1).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.01714), Sec 6.3-6.5
finding: Letting the model write its own relevant examples before solving beats 0-shot CoT and fixed few-shot CoT, and beats 5 retrieved train-set examples for larger models, but loses to retrieval for small models. With only 1 self-generated example the model leans on it too much.
numbers: GSM8K, 5-shot, accuracy by model scale (curie / davinci-001 / davinci-002 / davinci-003): 0-shot CoT 2/6/22/50 percent; 5-shot fixed CoT 2/10/43/54; 5-shot retrieved CoT 3/11/47/57; self-generated 2/9/48/61. GPT-3.5-turbo: self-generated GSM8K 77.8 (K=5) vs 76.1 (K=1); MATH 37.1 (K=5) vs 34.8 (K=1); K>=3 stable.
limits: Retrieved baseline is by similarity from the GSM8K train set, a clean bank. Older and mid-size models. No random-retrieved arm; fixed few-shot is the nearest control.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: gives a fixed-vs-retrieved contrast at k=5 (+3 points at davinci-003) and a k=1 weakness (-1.7 GSM8K, -2.3 MATH vs K=5 for self-generated). A self-generated example is a free competitor to a stored case.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2406.04271)
finding: Store distilled, generic thought templates, not raw solutions. Retrieve by embedding similarity between a distilled problem description and each template description. Removing the problem-distiller step lowers accuracy.
numbers: Claims on 10 tasks with GPT-4: +11% on Game of 24, +20% on Geometric Shapes, +51% on Checkmate-in-One over prior SOTA at about 12% of multi-query cost. Ablation: without the problem-distiller, both Llama3-70B and GPT-4 drop, more on Game of 24 and Checkmate-in-One than on MGSM or word sorting. Bar values appear only in figures; I did not read them.
limits: Author-side numbers; no retrieval-vs-random or key-comparison ablation (it changes key and content together). Templates are task-type level, so little per-instance retrieval.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: second line of evidence that a structure-level key helps on complex tasks and matters little on simple ones. Does not isolate key from stored content.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: case-based reasoning for retrieval augmented generation in LLMs for legal QA (arXiv 2404.04302)
finding: Case = question, support text, entities. Retrieval compared a weighted hybrid of the three parts [0.25, 0.40, 0.35] with single parts and three encoders. Weighted hybrid with the AnglE encoder gave the best retrieval F1 and generation score, but the margin over no retrieval is small.
numbers: ALQA synthetic legal QA, 32 test cases, Mistral-7B generator, cosine to reference answer. No-RAG 0.8967. k=3 hybrid AnglEBERT full case 0.9141 (+1.94%), significant vs No-RAG at 95% and vs hybrid BERT k=1 at 90%. k=1 hybrid AnglEBERT support-only 0.9121; BERT k=1 full case 0.9068; k=3 BERT 0.9007/0.8998. Best retrieval F1 at [0.25,0.40,0.35], k=3.
limits: Only 32 test cases, synthetic data built by GPT-4, a similarity score not a correctness score. Single-part weights were listed as comparators but the paper shows that comparison only as a heat map, so I cannot quote a clean weighted-vs-unweighted gap.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the only LLM-era use of Richter-style per-attribute weights that I opened. Effect is about 2% of a similarity metric and not clearly separated from encoder choice. Weights were hand-set, not learned.

source: Lu et al. (2022) Fantastically ordered prompts (ACL 2022, arXiv 2104.08786)
finding: Order of the same few examples swings accuracy from near state-of-the-art to near chance, across all sizes of GPT-2/GPT-3. Good orders do not transfer across models or tasks.
numbers: 4 samples, all 24 permutations, SST-2 and Subj: some permutations above 85% (comparable to supervised), others around 50% (chance). Entropy-based probing selection gave about 13% relative gain.
limits: GPT-2 and GPT-3 (up to 175B), classification, 4 examples; not 2025-26 frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: position matters at k=4 for older models. Still untested for 2025-26 models on 1-4 retrieved cases. If order matters, rank by similarity and test a reverse order once.

source: Peng et al. (2024) Revisiting demonstration selection strategies in in-context learning (ACL 2024, arXiv 2401.12087), Tables 2 and 5
finding: Nearest-neighbour (TopK) selection beats random, and the margin depends on model and data. Permuting the order of four chosen examples changes accuracy; TopK reduces but does not remove this variance.
numbers: GPT2-XL, 4 examples, 10 random permutations: SST-2 Random 68.8 (var 0.90), TopK 78.6 (0.56), their TopK+ConE 82.0 (0.26). Subj: 56.7 vs 86.2 vs 91.0. CR: 67.8 (var 4.00) vs 73.9 (0.61) vs 81.0. Winner between BM25 and TopK flips across GPT-J, Llama2-7B and Llama2-13B on SST-2.
limits: GPT2-XL and Llama2 era; classification and translation, not multi-step reasoning.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 9: a random control exists here at old scale: Random to TopK is 6 to 30 points on classification for GPT2-XL. Which retriever wins can flip with the model, so test per backbone.

source: Yoo et al. (2022) Ground-truth labels matter (EMNLP 2022 Findings, arXiv 2205.12685)
finding: Partial failed replication of Min et al. (2022). With a label-correctness sensitivity metric and a ground-truth label effect ratio, correct labels matter more or less depending on the setup. Template verbosity and model size are the controlling factors.
numbers: Abstract and introduction were read in detail; per-model values were not transcribed. The introduction says the gap between ground-truth and fully incorrect labels differs by setup, with prior work reporting very different gaps.
limits: Classification ICL with fixed demonstrations, GPT-2/GPT-J/GPT-3 class. Not retrieved near-duplicates.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: keeps K11 contested. Label noise in fixed demos costs little in some setups and a lot in others, so the Min et al. result cannot be trusted for retrieved near-copies. Xiong et al. (d05, d06) is closer evidence.

source: Gap note: not found despite search
finding: Not found: (a) any LLM-era test of adaptation-guided retrieval; (b) a random-case plus no-case control at k=1 for a 2025-26 frontier model on multi-step tasks; (c) the Wilkerson and Leake (ICCBR 2024, On implementing case-based reasoning with large language models, pp. 404-417) 20-28% agreement figure; (d) any ablation of per-attribute similarity weights against a single embedding with a correctness metric; (e) a 2025-26 position test on 1-4 short retrieved cases. Search was limited this session (WebSearch quota used up; arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned HTTP 429), so absence is only weak evidence.
limits: Follows from a rate-limited search, not a full literature scan.
agent_relevance: These are the experiments our own harness would have to run: k=1 similar vs random vs none; corrupted-label retrieved cases; AGR-style reranking by an LLM judge; key-type comparison; top-1 position swap.
